passages.text: An AluYa5 Insertion in the 3'UTR of COL4A1 and Cerebral Small Vessel Disease
This case-control study investigated gene variants associated with cerebral small vessel disease.
Key Points
Question
What are the missing gene variants in cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD)?
Findings

This 2-stage study involved linkage analysis among 2 large families, including 9 patients with CSVD, and a case-control study of 2 probands from these families and 244 unrelated probands; linkage analysis and next-generation sequencing identified a pathogenic AluYa5 insertion in COL4A1 3'UTR in the families, while the case-control study identified 7 carriers among 246 probands and none in the control group. This insertion was associated with an upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA and protein through perturbation of COL4A1 polyadenylation signals usage and with a severe autosomal dominant CSVD.
Meaning

This study found that a novel sequence variation event was associated with COL4A1 polyadenylation signals usage and severe CSVD through dysregulation of this major vascular matrisome gene, suggesting diagnostic and therapeutic implications.
Importance
Cerebral small vessel diseases (CSVDs) account for one-fifth of stroke cases. Numerous familial cases remain unresolved after routine screening of known CSVD genes.
Objective
To identify novel genes and mechanisms associated with familial CSVD.
Design, Setting, and Participants

This 2-stage study involved linkage analysis and a case-control study; linkage analysis and whole exome and genome sequencing were used to identify candidate gene variants in 2 large families with CSVD (9 patients with CSVD). Then, a case-control analysis was conducted on 246 unrelated probands, including probands from these 2 families and 244 additional probands. All probands (clinical onset <age 55 years and >=1 first-degree relative with CSVD) were referred to the French cerebrovascular referral center between 2013 and 2023. The large-scale gnomAD structural variant database and 467 healthy individuals of French ancestry were used as a control group.
Main Outcomes and Measures

A pathogenic AluYa5 insertion was identified within the COL4A1 3'UTR in the 2 large families with CSVD. Reverse transcriptase-quantitative polymerase chain reaction (RT-qPCR), Western blot, and long-read RNA sequencing were used to investigate outcomes associated with the insertion using patient fibroblasts. Clinical and magnetic resonance imaging features of probands with variants and available relatives were assessed.
Results

Among 246 probands (141 females [57.3%]; median [IQR] age at referral, 56 [49-64] years), 7 patients of French ancestry carried the insertion. This insertion was absent in 467 healthy French individuals in a control group (odds ratio,  ; 95% CI, 2.78 to  ; P = 5 x 10-4) and 10 847 individuals from the gnomAD structural variant database (odds ratio,  ; 95% CI, 64.77 to  ; P = 2.42 x 10-12). In these 7 patients' families, 19 family members with CSVD carried the insertion. RT-qPCR and Western blot showed an upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA (10.6-fold increase; 95% CI, 1.4-fold to 17.1-fold increase) and protein levels (2.8-fold increase; 95% CI, 2.1-fold to 3.5-fold increase) in patient vs control group fibroblasts. Long-read RNA sequencing data showed that the insertion was associated with perturbation in the use of canonical COL4A1 polyadenylation signals (approximately 87% of isoforms transcribed from the wild type allele vs 5% of isoforms transcribed from the allele with the insertion used the 2 distal canonical polyadenylation signals). The main clinical feature of individuals with CSVD was the recurrence of pontine ischemic lesions starting at an early age (17 of 19 patients [89.5%]).
Conclusions and relevance

This study found a novel mechanism associated with COL4A1 upregulation and a highly penetrant adult-onset CSVD. These findings suggest that quantitative alterations of the cerebrovascular matrisome are associated with CSVD pathogenesis, with diagnostic and therapeutic implications.
Introduction

Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) consists of a heterogeneous group of disorders accounting for one-fifth of stroke cases worldwide. It is also the second leading cause of dementia. Most CSVDs are sporadic and associated with age and hypertension, but several monogenic forms of the disease have been reported. The most frequent one is cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. In addition to its diagnostic applications, identification of causative variants has proven to be a powerful approach to decipher CSVD mechanisms. However, in most patients with familial CSVD, the cause remains elusive, precluding genetic counseling and mechanistic studies. Indeed, targeted sequencing of exons and exon-intron boundaries of all known CSVD genes does not identify a causative variant in almost 80% of familial CSVD cases. This strongly suggests that other genes or noncoding variants may be involved in CSVD.

Linkage analysis performed on large multiplex families in combination with Sanger sequencing led to the discovery of genes involved in numerous monogenic diseases. The development of whole exome sequencing (WES) and whole genome sequencing (WGS) substantially shortened this approach.

In this study, we combined linkage analysis, WES, and WGS to identify candidate variants in 2 French families with multiple cases of CSVD. We then designed a case-control study to search for statistical association using probands from these 2 families, 244 additional unrelated probands with CSVD, and 467 healthy French individuals in a control group. We also used the large-scale gnomAD structural variant database as a control.
Methods

All procedures and protocols for this 2-stage study involving linkage analysis and a case-control study complied with the Institut National de la Sante Et de la Recherche Medicale human investigation committee and institutional review board. All patients provided a written informed consent for participation in genetic studies in accordance with French ethical recommendations for genetic study. Consent forms signed by the patients allow the publication of all clinical and MRI information, except photographs and video and audio recordings of patients. This study followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (STROBE) reporting guideline for observational studies.

There were 2 families (F1 and F2), including 3 members in F1 and 7 members in F2 (Figure 1) showing ischemic stroke manifestations and white matter lesions strongly suggestive of a CSVD. They were referred to the French Reference Cerebrovascular Diseases Genetics Lab (Saint-Louis Hospital, Paris). Targeted sequencing of known CSVD genes was performed in F1 and F2 probands. We included 244 additional CSVD probands based on the following criteria: (1) presence of a vascular leukoencephalopathy strongly suggestive of a CSVD; (2) no pathogenic variants detected with our CSVD-targeted gene panel, which includes NOTCH3, HTRA1, COL4A1, COL4A2, TREX1, GLA, CTSA, APP, and LAMB1; (3) age at clinical onset younger than 55 years; and (4) 1 or more first-degree relative with a clinical history of stroke, vascular dementia, or both.
Genealogical Trees of Families F1 to F7
CSVD indicates cerebral small vessel disease; MRI, magnetic resonance imaging.

We performed linkage analysis of families F1 and F2 and WES of F1 and F2 family members and 244 additional probands with CSVD as described in the eMethods in Supplement 1. To further investigate structural and regulatory noncoding variants present in possibly linked regions, we performed WGS of the 3 F1 patients (eMethods in Supplement 1).

Copy number variants and structural variations, including mobile element insertions (MEIs), were searched from Illumina single-nucleotide variation (formerly, single-nucleotide polymorphism) arrays and WGS data as described in the eMethods in Supplement 1. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and Sanger sequencing (protocols available upon request) were used to confirm the candidate MEI, and PCR was used to genotype this MEI in all 244 probands with CSVD and in 467 healthy French individuals in the control group. In addition, the GnomAD structural variant database version 2.1 was used as a control database for structural variations.

Skin fibroblasts were obtained from patients F1-8 and F2-12 and from an additional proband (F8-16) (eFigure 1 in Supplement 1) referred for targeted sequencing and in whom PCR analysis detected the candidate MEI insertion. Of note, proband F8 was identified after the completion of the initial study and was therefore not included in the case-control study. The search for the insertion using PCR was performed in this proband based on clinical, familial, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) similarities with previously identified AluYa5 carriers. In addition, we obtained skin fibroblasts from 4 healthy individuals in a control group (C1-C4) (CBC Biotech), 1 patient with CSVD and a COL4A1 duplication, and 5 patients with CSVD who did not carry the insertion. These fibroblasts were used for reverse transcriptase-quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), Western blotting, and long-read RNA sequencing (eMethods in Supplement 1). Details on library preparation, sequencing, and alignment according to the Oxford Nanopore technology are presented in the eMethods in Supplement 1. The aim was to investigate alternative polyadenylation signal (PAS) usage depending on the presence or absence of the MEI in the 3'UTR of COL4A1 (eMethods in Supplement 1).
Statistical Analysis

The number of carriers of the candidate AluYa5 insertion was compared between patients with CSVD and those in the control group using the Fisher exact test implemented in R statistical software version 4.2 (R Project for Statistical Computing). We compared mRNA and protein levels between patients with CSVD and those in the control group using the Mann-Whitney test using Prism software version 9 (GraphPad). Differential use of polyadenylation sites between patients and those in the control group was analyzed with a Mann-Whitney test using R statistical software version 4.2. A 2-sided P value < .05 was considered statistically significant.
Results
Baseline Characteristics of Study Participants

The 2 large families used for linkage analysis were of French ancestry and included 9 patients with CSVD who had blood samples (3 females [33.3%]; median [IQR] age, 50 [42-59] years). Their genealogical trees are presented in Figure 1. Including 2 probands from the 2 families with CSVD and 244 additional probands, a total of 246 probands (141 females [57.3%]; median [IQR] age at referral, 56 [49-64] years) were used for the case-control study; among them, 227 individuals (92.2%) were of European ancestry. Proband age at clinical onset was younger than 55 years, and probands had at least 1first-degree relative with CSVD.
Clinical and Neuroimaging Features of Patients in Families F1 and F2

Genealogical trees and clinical and MRI features of F1 and F2 family members are presented in Figure 1, Figure 2, and Figure 3 and eTables 1 and 2 in Supplement 1. Probands F1-8 and F2-9 were referred for targeted CSVD gene screening and remained negative. We investigated 2 additional members of family F1 and 5 additional members of family F2, obtaining clinical and MRI data. In total, blood samples were taken from 9 individuals with CSVD in these 2 families.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Data of Patients From Family F1

The first column presents sagittal T1-weighted images. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images are presented in columns 2 to 4. All patients present pontine infarcts and a vascular leukoencephalopathy associated with hemispheric lacunes.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging Data of Patients From Family F2

The first column presents sagittal T1-weighted images except for C (patient F2-12), which presents diffusion-weighted images. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images are presented in columns 2 to 4, except for A (patient F2-9) and B (patient F2-10) in column 4, which present gradient echo sequences, and D (patient F2-11) in column 3, which presents sagittal T1 images. All patients except patient F2-9 (A) present pontine infarcts and vascular leukoencephalopathy associated with hemispheric lacunes.
Family F1

Patient F1-8 (proband) was a male aged 45 years without any vascular risk factor. At age 39 years, he experienced sudden dizziness, paresthesia of the left arm, left central facial palsy, and dysarthria related to a pontine ischemic lesion. At ages 41 and 43 years, he had sudden transient diplopia without any incident lesion on MRI. In the following years, he reported mild cognitive disturbances.

His female first cousin aged 45 years (F1-9) had a well-controlled hypertension under monotherapy but no other vascular risk factor. At age 35 years, she presented a sudden episode of hemisensory loss related to a pontine ischemic lesion. At age 41 years, she had a similar episode. MRI showed an extension of the previous pontine ischemic lesion and an additional punctiform white matter hyperintensity in the centrum semioval.

Their uncle (F1-7) was an active smoker and already experienced myocardial infarction. At age 42 years, he twice presented a sudden episode of loss of balance and dysphonia associated with headache. MRI showed a pontine ischemic lesion. In the 2 following years, he developed a progressive cognitive deterioration and dementia, without any stroke event. He was treated for a primary cerebral vasculitis with cyclophosphamide and corticosteroid for 2 years.

MRI data for these 3 patients are presented in Figure 2. We detected 1 or several lacunes in the pons, subcortical hemispheric area, or both in all these patients. Hemispheric white matter hyperintensities were present in all patients, in the centrum semioval, subcortical, and periventricular areas. Anterior temporal lobes, thalami, and external capsules were involved in the 2 most severe cases. Gradient echo images, available in only F1-9, did not detect any microbleed.

In addition to these 3 patients, 3 additional patients (F1-4, F1-5, and F1-2) were assessed using clinical health records. The proband's mother (F1-4) presented at ages 49 and 51 years with 2 episodes of sudden loss of balance and vertical diplopia and developed cognitive impairment. F1-5, another uncle of the proband, presented with a stepwise motor and cognitive deterioration up to a motor disability with dementia. He was treated for a long time as having progressive multiple sclerosis. F1-2, the grandmother of the proband, had a history of early severe cognitive impairment. F1-4, F1-5, and F1-2 died prematurely at ages 53, 62, and 50 years, respectively.
Family F2

Proband F2-9, a male aged 55 years, had several vascular risk factors, including hypertension (well-controlled by treatment), dyslipidemia, active smoking, and alcoholism. He complained with chronic headache and developed a stepwise cognitive decline from age 50 years. Cognitive testing showed alteration of performance, possibly increased by an anxiety disorder, in tests evaluating attention, processing speed, and verbal episodic memory. No sudden focal symptom was ever observed. His first MRI (at age 53 years) showed a recent ischemic lesion in the right lenticular nucleus. In 2022, he experienced diplopia (sixth nerve palsy) and gait disturbance.

Patient F2-10 experienced a transient episode of diplopia at age 42 years and a partial third nerve palsy at age 45 years, both related to pontine ischemic lesions. At ages 46 and 49 years, he presented a sudden hemiparesis related to incident ischemic lesions in the centrum semioval and internal capsule. He was treated for 4 years as having progressive multiple sclerosis. At age 56 years, he died because of a severe deep intracerebral hemorrhage.

There were 4 other first cousins of F2-9 who were investigated and underwent MRI and blood sampling. Patient F2-11 presented at age 54 years with a sudden diplopia, ptosis, and loss of balance related to a recent pontine ischemic lesion. At age 59 years, patient F2-12 experienced a sudden episode of transient third nerve palsy with loss of balance. At age 59 years, patient F2-13 presented a pontine infarct. Patient F2-16 experienced an episode of numbness of the left hemibody with sudden gait disturbance at age 60 years.

Of these 6 patients, 5 individuals presented lacunes located in the pons, including 3 patients with multiple pontine ischemic lesions. The sixth patient (F2-12) had no pontine lesion but experienced symptoms evocative of vertebrobasilar territory transient ischemic attack. There were 4 patients with lacunes located in the subcortical hemispheric area. Hemispheric white matter hyperintensities were observed in all 6 patients, although with variable magnitude. No abnormalities were observed in the anterior temporal lobes. Gradient echo images, available in all patients, showed microbleeds in 1 patient (F2-10) in the deep supratentorial gray matter, deep cerebellum, and brainstem.

Clinical health records were obtained for 2 additional patients. Patient F2-14 had a vascular leukoencephalopathy and died prematurely at age 55 years. Patient F2-15 died prematurely at 56 years of a cerebral hemorrhage.
Linkage Analysis and WES Data

We identified 35 and 22 possibly linked regions for family F1 and F2, respectively (eFigures 2-3 in Supplement 1). Our WES filtering strategy identified 1 variant fulfilling our pathogenicity criteria (eMethods in Supplement 1). This variant, detected in F2, was located in a zinc transporter gene expressed in the mammary gland and was therefore not further considered. Linkage analysis revealed that the families shared a 4.8-Mb possibly-linked region on 13q33-34, a locus containing COL4A1 and COL4A2. In cDNA sequencing of COL4A1 and COL4A2, both alleles were expressed and normal in patients F1-8 and F2-12. Altogether, these data suggested that a noncoding sequence variation may have been located at the COL4A1/COL4A2 locus.
WGS Data Analysis

WGS did not detect any pathogenic variant in the COL4A1/COL4A2 promoter region. Structural variant search using Delly, Lumpy, and Manta was negative within the COL4A1/COL4A2 region and in other linked regions. Careful visualization of reads aligned within the COL4A1/COL4A2 locus revealed the presence of an insertion, which was exclusively supported by soft-clipped reads, in the 3'UTR of COL4A1 (eFigure 4 in Supplement 1). The insertion at position chr13:110149065 (hg38) best matched to the consensus sequence of AluYa5, with the presence of 2 single substitutions (C110T and A189G). The insertion was validated by PCR, Sanger sequencing, and long-read RNA sequencing (eFigures 5-6 in Supplement 1).
AluYa5 Insertion in 3'UTR of COL4A1 and CSVD

In addition to patients from F1 and F2, 5 additional probands with CSVD who were unrelated also had the insertion. Results were confirmed by PCR and Sanger sequencing. We conducted PCR genotyping on 467 healthy French individuals in a control group to evaluate the prevalence of this genetic variant within the healthy French population to exclude that it may be a benign polymorphism in the French population. All individuals in this control group tested negative for the variant (odds ratio,  ; 95% CI, 2.78 to  ; P = 5 x 10-4), suggesting its rarity or absence in the general French population. Furthermore, we investigated the presence of our insertion in the gnomAD structural variant database version 2.1, in which the same software (ie, MELT) was used to identify Alu insertions. The insertion was not found in 10 847 well-covered genomes in the 3'UTR of COL4A1 (odds ratio,  ; 95% CI, 64.77 to  ; P = 2.42 x 10-12).
Upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA and Protein in Carriers of AluYa5

To study functional outcomes associated with the AluYa5 insertion, we compared COL4A1 mRNA and protein levels in fibroblasts from patients F1-8 and F2-12, healthy individuals C1 to C4 in a control group, a COL4A1/2 duplicated patient, and a CSVD patient without the insertion as a control. RT-qPCR showed a 10.6-fold (95% CI, 1.4-fold to 17.1-fold) increase of COL4A1 mRNA levels in patients F1-8 and F2-12 vs individuals in the control group (eFigure 7 in Supplement 1).

Protein levels of COL4A1 were also significantly higher in fibroblast lysates (2.8-fold; 95% CI, 2.1-fold to 3.5-fold increase) and conditioned media (2.9-fold; 95% CI, 2.4-fold to 3.3-fold increase) from patients with the insertion compared with 4 healthy individuals in the control group. These levels were comparable with those detected in the duplicated patient who served as a control (Figure 4).
Western Blot Analysis of Wild-Type and Variant COL4A1 Expressed in Transfected Cells and Endogenous Fibroblasts

A-B, A Western blot of conditioned medium and cell lysates from HEK293T cells transfected with wild type and variant COL4A1 and human skin fibroblasts from 4 healthy individuals in the control group (C1-C4), 2 patients carrying the AluYa5 insertion (P1-P2), and 1 patient duplicated at the COL4A1/2 locus. A, In the top panel, blot n 1 was probed with an anticollagen IV antibody, and in the middle and bottom panels, blot n 2 was probed with antifibronectin and anti-MMP2 antibodies used as loading controls (see antibody references in the eMethods in Supplement 1). C-D, Visualizations of relative protein expression levels are presented from A and B, respectively. Circles indicate COL4-dup, the patient duplicated at the COL4A1/2 locus; HEK, HEK293T cells; horizontal lines, means; MW, molecular weight; NT, nontransfected plasmid; pCMV-Col4a1, plasmid-expressing COL4A1; squares, patients with AluYa5 insertion; triangles, control group.
AluYa5 Insertion and PAS Usage

Based on the location of this insertion within the 3'UTR region, we raised the hypothesis that it may have been associated with disruption of COL4A1 PAS usage. The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) lists 2 PASs for COL4A1; the major one is located at position c.6421 (designated in Figure 5 as c.*1281 based on its distance to the stop codon) and the second one at position c.6513 (c.*1373). PAS databases (eg, PolyA_DB3) list more than 10 PASs for COL4A1. We used long-read RNA sequencing of 3 patients with the insertion (F1-8, F2-12, and F8-16) and 7 individuals in a control group (4 healthy individuals and 3 patients with CSVD without the insertion) to investigate the usage of PASs in these individuals, finding that 6 isoforms of COL4A1 could be identified depending on PAS usage (eFigure 8 in Supplement 1). They differed in their 3'UTR size. Among 7 individuals in the control group, mainly 2 isoforms using the 2 distal canonical PASs listed in NCBI were expressed, with approximately 42% use of the c.*1281 PAS and approximately 43% use of the c.*1373 PAS (Figure 5). In contrast, 3 patients with the insertion expressed equally 4 isoforms, with approximately 23% usage of each of 2 distal PASs (c.*1281 and c.*1373) but also approximately 20% usage of c.*236 and c.*711 proximal sites. We detected 2 other isoforms (c.*610 and c.*920) at an approximately 7% level in the patients that were not expressed or were expressed at a very low level in individuals in the control group (Figure 5).
AluYa5 Insertion and Polyadenylation Signal (PAS) Usage

A, The diagram shows the last exon and 3'UTR of COL4A1 with the 6 PAS annotated as c.*distance to the stop codon. B, The diagram of the 3'UTR shows the 6 possible isoforms depending on PAS usage. The 6 isoforms differ only by the length of their 3'UTR. Cleavage and polyadenylation start approximately 15 to 30 bp downstream of the PAS. C, Proportions of expressed isoforms depending on PAS usage are shown in 3 patients carrying the insertion and 7 individuals in the control group. D, Proportions of each of expressed isoform by the wild type and variant allele depending on PAS usage in patients F2-12 and F8-16 are presented. T_AluYa5+ represents isoforms transcribed from the allele that carries the AluYa5 insertion. G_AluYa5- represents isoforms transcribed from the wild type allele.

In addition, we took advantage of a heterozygous polymorphism present in COL4A1 exon 45 (rs3742207-T/G) in patients F2-12 and F8-16 to quantify transcripts encoded by the wild type allele and inserted allele using long-read RNA sequencing data. The insertion occurred on the same haplotype as the T allele (T_AluYa5 haplotype). Proportions of isoforms produced by the T_AluYa5 allele were as follows: approximately 43% c.*236, approximately 10% c.*601, approximately 29% c.*711, and approximately 13% c.*920; approximately 5% of transcripts used the 2 distal signals c.*1281 and c.*1373. Proportions of isoforms produced by the wild type allele (G allele/no-AluYa5 insertion) were similar to those observed in the control group; approximately 87% of isoforms used the 2 canonical distal PASs. The remaining approximately 13% of isoforms used the 4 other PASs (Figure 5). Altogether, these RNA sequencing and expression data suggest that the Alu insertion was associated with changes in usage of PAS and an upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA and protein levels.
Clinical and Neuroimaging Features of F3-F7 Patients

Genealogical trees and clinical and MRI features of F3 to F7 probands and relatives are presented in Figure 1 and eFigure 9 and eTables 3 to 4 in Supplement 1. Familial history was suggestive of an autosomal dominant inheritance in all families (Figure 1). Clinical and MRI features were similar to those observed in families F1 and F2, with pontine involvement and hemispheric multiple ischemic lesions associated with hemispheric white matter hypersignals in most patients (9 of 10 patients [90.0%]). Recurrent pontine and subcortical ischemic lesions started at a mean (SD) age of 50 (9) years (eTables 1-4 in Supplement 1) among 17 of 19 patients (89.5%). A younger age at onset (<50 years) was observed in 9 of 19 patients. However, microbleeds were more frequent in patients from families F3 to F7. Intracerebral hemorrhage was observed in patients F2-10, F2-15, F5-5, and F5-10.
Discussion

In this 2-stage study with linkage analysis and a case-control study, we identified an Alu insertion in the 3'UTR noncoding region of COL4A1 in 7 families with a disabling autosomal dominant CSVD. This insertion was associated with a strong upregulation of COL4A1 through a change in PAS usage.

Several results support the association of this AluYa5 insertion with CSVD. First, the insertion was absent from the gnomAD structural variant large-scale control database. Second, this insertion was co-segregating with the affected phenotype in all 7 families. Third, this insertion was associated with a strong upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA and protein levels, reminiscent of pontine autosomal dominant microangiopathy arteriopathy with leukoencephalopathy (PADMAL), another severe CSVD caused by a sequence variation in a COL4A1 microRNA binding site (miR29).

annotations.text: pontine autosomal dominant microangiopathy arteriopathy with leukoencephalopathy

passages.text: Clinical features of patients from these families were characterized by the recurrence of pontine and subcortical ischemic lesions starting at a mean (SD) age of 50 (9) years, and 9 of 19 patients investigated so far had an age of onset younger than 50 years. The high frequency of pontine infarcts has also been observed in PADMAL. However, microbleeds (and to a lower degree, intracerebral hemorrhage, as observed in patients F2-10, F2-15, F5-5, and F5-10) may be more frequent in this condition associated with the AluYa5 insertion. Interestingly, COL4A1 duplications have also been associated with a similar phenotype. Altogether, these data strongly suggest that COL4A1 noncoding sequence variations should be searched in unresolved familial CSVD cases with pontine infarcts and leukoencephalopathy. This search should combine copy number analysis and 3'UTR screening. When negative, an upregulation of COL4A1 in patient fibroblasts should be assessed using RT-qPCR and Western-blotting. In case of an upregulation, full sequencing of all noncoding regions should be performed given that other mechanisms may lead to gene upregulation.

The Alu insertion identified in these 7 families was associated with strong upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA and associated with a change in PAS usage in the 3'UTR of this gene. RNA processing is an essential step in gene regulation. It involves an RNA endonucleolytic cleavage followed by the addition of a poly(A) tail, which allows the translocation of the nascent mRNA from the nucleus to the cytoplasm and the regulation of translation efficiency and RNA degradation. This tightly regulated process fine-tunes gene expression in a cell type and cellular state-dependent manner. Various loss and gain of function alterations have been reported to be associated with dysregulation of alternative polyadenylation and disease, including endocrine, oncological, immunological, and neurological diseases. As an example, sequence variants in the proximal canonical PAS of the NAA10 gene lead to an increase in usage of a distal PASs and a 50% decrease in mRNA expression. In contrast, a variant creating a canonical proximal PAS in IRF5 shifts polyadenylation from the distal canonical PAS, leading to increased expression of IRF5. The AluYa5 insertion observed in our patients is located downstream of the major canonical distal PAS of COL4A1, which is associated with an almost complete abolition of this canonical distal PAS usage and the use of 2 proximal PASs, leading to the expression of shorter 3'UTR isoforms of COL4A1 and upregulation of COL4A1 mRNA. Suggesting how this preferential usage of these proximal PAS may be associated with COL4A1 upregulation would be speculative at this point. However, several lines of evidence obtained in other diseases and cellular models strongly suggest that this upregulation may be an outcome associated with the deletion of regulatory regions in shorter 3'UTRs.
Limitations

This study has several limitations. The number of patients in these 7 families is still limited, and the description of all phenotypic features of this condition will need the recruitment of additional families. A search for a founding effect will also be needed. This study is monocentric and focused on a singular population. Analysis of other populations is warranted. Nonetheless, this study demonstrates the power of combining linkage analysis of families with several members who have a rare CSVD with WES and WGS from a large series of unrelated probands.
Conclusions

In this 2-stage study involving linkage analysis of 2 large families and a case-control study of 246 unrelated probands, we found an association between an AluYa5 insertion located in a COL4A1 3'UTR and CSVD. We also uncovered a novel mechanism associated with COL4A1 expression. This discovery suggests the possibility that other, yet-unidentified noncoding anomalies contributing to COL4A1 upregulation may be responsible for additional familial cases that remain unresolved.

passages.text: Dual-responsive nanocarriers for efficient cytosolic protein delivery and CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy of inflammatory skin disorders

Developing protein drugs that can target intracellular sites remains a challenge due to their inadequate membrane permeability. Efficient carriers for cytosolic protein delivery are required for protein-based drugs, cancer vaccines, and CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapies. Here, we report a screening process to identify highly efficient materials for cytosolic protein delivery from a library of dual-functionalized polymers bearing both boronate and lipoic acid moieties. Both ligands were found to be crucial for protein binding, endosomal escape, and intracellular protein release. Polymers with higher grafting ratios exhibit remarkable efficacies in cytosolic protein delivery including enzymes, monoclonal antibodies, and Cas9 ribonucleoprotein while preserving their activity. Optimal polymer successfully delivered Cas9 ribonucleoprotein targeting NLRP3 to disrupt NLRP3 inflammasomes in vivo and ameliorate inflammation in a mouse model of psoriasis. Our study presents a promising option for the discovery of highly efficient materials tailored for cytosolic delivery of specific proteins and complexes such as Cas9 ribonucleoprotein.
A polymer library enables efficient delivery of proteins and CRISPR-Cas9 gene therapy to treat inflammatory skin disorders.
INTRODUCTION

Protein-based therapeutics have gained enormous attention in the pharmaceutical market. Since the approval of recombinant human insulin by the Food and Drug Administration in 1982 for the treatment of diabetes mellitus marked a pivotal milestone, a rapidly growing number of protein drugs including monoclonal antibodies, cytokines, enzymes, and peptides have been launched, which accounts for nearly 50% of the top 10 and top 200 biggest selling drugs globally in 2022. The great interest in protein drugs is predominantly ascribed to their higher potency, stronger selectivity, and lower adverse effects compared with small-molecule drugs. A notable limitation of currently approved protein drugs is their predominantly extracellular target specificity due to the inherent membrane-impermeability characteristic of proteins, which hampers their ability to effectively access intracellular targets. As a result, developing protein drugs that can efficiently act on intracellular targets remains a crucial challenge in the field of therapeutics. Overcoming this hurdle would greatly expand the scope and potential applications of protein-based therapies. Besides, emerging biotechnologies such as CRISPR-associated protein 9 (CRISPR-Cas9)-mediated genome editing require the development of efficient tools to directly transport Cas9 ribonucleoprotein (RNP) into the nucleus of target cells.

During the past decade, numerous viral and nonviral delivery systems have been developed for Cas9 RNP-mediated gene editing. Viral vectors usually have high delivery efficiency but are associated with potential risks of immune responses, genome integration, and the activation of cancer-related genes. Alternatively, nonviral carriers such as lipids, inorganic nanoparticles, and polymers with higher safety have been widely used in the delivery of Cas9 RNP for genome editing recently. However, several challenges still need to be addressed. First, Cas9 RNP has limited binding affinity with the nonviral carriers, and negatively supercharged Cas9 proteins such as 20-mer glutamate-tagged Cas9 (E20-Cas9) and GFP-tagged Cas9 (GFP-Cas9) are usually used to enhance their binding with the carriers. However, the supercharged tags not only bring complicated biosynthesis but may also affect the bioactivity of Cas9. Second, the responsive release of Cas9 RNP from the carrier after cytosolic delivery is another challenge for the delivery system to achieve efficient nuclear entry and genome editing. Last, the in vivo gene editing efficiency and therapeutic performance of the Cas9 RNP delivery systems on different disease models need further investigations to promote their clinical translation.

In this study, screening for efficient carriers for cytosolic protein and Cas9 RNP delivery from a library of dual-responsive polymers can contribute significantly to the field of gene editing and protein delivery. The polymers were synthesized by grafting various contents of phenylboronate and lipoic acid (LA) moieties ligands on a polyamidoamine dendrimer. Phenylboronate has been reported to stabilize the polymer/protein complexes for cytosolic protein delivery via nitrogen-boronate coordination with lysine or histidine residues on proteins, while LA is an endogenous natural small molecule that participates in various biochemical reactions in the body, such as tricarboxylic acid cycle, mitochondrial energy metabolism, and stability regulation of multienzyme complexes. LA has remarkable antioxidant properties, which can eliminate free radicals and other oxides, protecting cells from oxidative stress damage. Thus, LA is widely used as an anti-inflammatory drug for the treatment of Alzheimer's disease and diabetes. In addition to being directly used as a small molecule drug, LA is also extensively used in biomaterials. LA not only provides better stability for biomaterials but also increases their versatility. Because of its distinctive structure, amphiphilic LA can be easily conjugated onto the surface of polymers via acylation reactions. The hydrophobic five-membered cyclic structure is beneficial for the formation of core-shell micelles in aqueous solution, which can be disintegrated under intracellular glutathione (GSH) reduction conditions, resulting in the release of cargo drugs. LA-based biomaterials can form disulfide bonds with free thiol groups on the cell surface, thereby entering cells through thiol-disulfide exchange-mediated cellular uptake, especially for cell-penetrating poly(disulfide)s. The cross-linking effect of LA is also applied to the construction of nanogel and hydrogel and hydrogel. The dendrimer was decorated with 4-nitrophenyl 4-(4,4,5,5-tetramethyl-1,3,2-dioxaborolan-2-yl)benzyl carbonate (NBC) and LA at different ratios, providing a library of dual-responsive polymers G5 dendrimer modified with boronate and LA (GBLA) in Fig. 1A. In addition, carriers with the optimal delivery efficiency can be screened from the GBLA polymer library for specific proteins, such as enhanced yellow fluorescent protein (eYFP), beta-galactosidase (beta-Gal), immunoglobulin G (IgG), and Cas9 RNP (Fig. 1B). Last, the carrier GBLA-22 with the highest delivery efficiency of Cas9 RNP was used for the treatment of model mice with psoriasis by targeting NLRP3 inflammasomes. As a result, the expression levels of psoriasis-related inflammatory cytokines were also significantly down-regulated in vivo and the psoriasis symptoms of mice markedly were ameliorated (Fig. 1C).

RESULTS
Construction of GBLA polymer carrier library

The ligand NBC was synthesized by reacting 4-(hydroxymethyl)phenylboronic acid pinacol ester with 4-nitrophenyl carbonochloridate and characterized by 1H nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR; fig. S1). Then, the NBC was modified on the surface of the generation 5 polyamidoamine dendrimer at different feeding molar ratios (fig. S2). A series of NBC-modified dendrimers were acquired, and the average numbers of NBC conjugated on each dendrimer were calculated to be 11, 23, 31, 40, and 47 according to 1H NMR analysis, respectively. These dendrimers were named GB-1, GB-2, GB-3, GB-4, and GB-5, corresponding to the increasing numbers of NBC conjugated to the dendrimers. LA anhydride (LAA) was then prepared (fig. S3) and further reacted with unmodified dendrimer or NBC-decorated dendrimers at different feeding molar ratios. A total number of 23 functionalized polymers were obtained, and the products were termed GBLA-1 to GBLA-23, respectively (Fig. 1A and figs. S4 to S9). The average numbers of NBC and LA on GBLA polymers are shown in table S1.
Cytosolic delivery of eYFP

The synthesized polymers in cytosolic protein delivery were then tested on HeLa cells using eYFP as a model protein. As shown in Fig. 2A and fig. S10, the protein delivery efficacy of GBLA polymers increases with higher grafting ratios of NBC and LA on the dendrimer. Among the polymers, GBLA-19 exhibited the most superior performance in the cytosolic delivery of eYFP. The cells treated with GBLA-19/eYFP showed well-dispersed yellow fluorescence throughout the cells, suggesting sufficient protein release after cell internalization. GBLA-19 showed markedly higher efficacy than mono-functionalized polymers such as LA-modified dendrimer (GBLA-3) and NBC-modified dendrimer (GBLA-17) with similar grafting ratios (Fig. 2B). These results clearly demonstrated that both chemical modifications play essential roles in cytosolic protein delivery. To further investigate the reason why GBLA-19 outperforms GBLA-3 and GBLA-17, we first characterized the polymer/protein complexes using dynamic light scattering (DLS). As shown in Fig. 2 (C and D), although nanoparticles complexed between four polymers and eYFP were formed with a surface potential of around 30 mV, GBLA-17/eYFP and GBLA-19/eYFP form uniform nanoparticles around 300 nm, which were much smaller than those by GBLA-3 and unmodified dendrimer GBLA-1. This result confirmed the beneficial role of phenylboronate modification in protein binding. The successful co-assembly of GBLA-19 and eYFP into nanoparticles was further identified by transmission electron microscopy (TEM). In addition, the protein loading efficiency of four representative polymers was quantitatively measured in both aqueous and phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) buffer solutions (Fig. 2E). All the investigated materials bound nearly 90% of feeding eYFP in water. However, the eYFP loading efficiencies of GBLA-1 and GBLA-3 decreased to about 20% in PBS buffer due to the weakened ionic interactions between dendrimer and eYFP by salt. In comparison, NBC-modified dendrimers GBLA-17 and GBLA-19 showed much-increased salt tolerance via the proposed nitrogen-boronate coordination, and the protein loading efficiencies reached about 66 and 80% in PBS, respectively. After conversion, it is equivalent to 53 and 65% of proteins loaded per mass of polymer. Meanwhile, it is noteworthy that GBLA-19 showed the highest salt tolerance among the polymers, which is probably due to the formation of cross-linking network by LA. To prove this, an ultraviolet-visible (UV-Vis) spectrum was performed to detect the polymer absorbance at 330 nm, which is the characteristic peak of a five-membered lipoyl ring. In fig. S11, it is mentioned that no obvious absorption peak at 330 nm was observed for GBLA-19 compared with GBLA-17. More directly, SDS-polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (SDS-PAGE) was conducted to observe the cross-linked dendrimers. As results presented in Fig. 2F, several bands at higher molecular weights were observed for GBLA-19, which confirms the cross-linking of LA moieties in GBLA-19 to form polymer aggregates. In comparison, no band for cross-linked polymers was observed for GBLA-17, suggesting that the cross-linking structure was caused by LA moieties in the polymer. Considering the responsiveness of NBC ligand to hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and the reduction responsiveness of the disulfide bond, the protein release from GBLA-19 under 5 mM H2O2 or 5 mM GSH was quantitatively tested according to the standard curve (fig. S12) by a fluorescence spectrophotometer. As shown in Fig. 2G, the released ratio of eYFP bound by GBLA-19 was nearly 20% in PBS buffer, which increased to 38% in the presence of 5 mM GSH. The increased protein release is triggered by the cleavage of the disulfide bond by GSH. On the other hand, nearly 62% bound eYFP by GBLA-19 was released in the presence of 5 mM H2O2. The markedly increased protein release under H2O2 is caused by the oxidization of NBC groups on the polymer (fig. S13). Together, the introduction of both NBC and LA ligands significantly increased the nanoparticle stability and allowed efficient cargo release triggered by GSH and H2O2. We also evaluated the cytotoxicity of the four polymers on HeLa cells (Fig. 2H). Compared with unmodified dendrimer GBLA-1, the other three carriers showed much-decreased cytotoxicity, which maintained more than 90% cell viability at concentrations up to 80 mug/ml. This phenomenon can be attributed to the reduction in charge density resulting from the conversion of the positively charged amino groups on the dendrimer surface into neutral NBC and LA functional groups.

Studies of endocytosis and endosomal escape

The endocytosis mechanism and endosomal escape of GBLA-19/eYFP in HeLa cells were further investigated. Time-dependent endocytosis of GBLA-19/eYFP was first investigated. As shown in fig. S14, the internalization of the GBLA-19/eYFP complex reached the maximum at 4 hours after incubation. The endocytosis pathway of the GBLA-19/eYFP complex on HeLa cells was further investigated using specific endocytosis inhibitors before nanoparticle incubation (Fig. 3, A and B). The cellular uptake of the GBLA-19/eYFP complex was completely inhibited at 4 C, suggesting that the internalization was energy-dependent. Methyl-beta-cyclodextrin (MbetaCD), a cholesterol-depleting reagent, also markedly decreased the cell uptake by 97%. In comparison, the endocytosis pretreated by cytochalasin D (Cyto D; an inhibitor of micropinocytosis), genistein (Gen; an inhibitor of caveolae-dependent pathways), chlorpromazine (CPZ; an inhibitor of clathrin-dependent pathways), and 5,5'-dithiobis(2-nitrobenzoic acid) (DTNB; a blocker of thiol-disulfide exchange-mediated pathways) showed negligible inhibitory effect. To further validate its endocytosis mediated by lipid rafts into cells, colocalization with lipid raft was quantified using a lipid raft labeling kit (catalog no. V34404 from Invitrogen) and the data are presented in fig. S15. As one of the main components of the reagent kit, Alexa Fluor 555 conjugate of cholera toxin subunit B (CT-B Fluor 555) can bind to the pentasaccharide chain of plasma membrane ganglioside GM1, which selectively partitions into lipid rafts. HeLa cells after treatment with GBLA-19-Cy5 for 2 hours were stained by CT-B Fluor 555 and anti-CT-B antibody to induce cross-linking. A green pseudo-color was assigned to the Cy5 channel to better observe the colocalization. The result showed that obvious yellow colocalization spots can be observed in cells, and Pearson's correlation coefficient reached 0.60 according to the two-dimensional intensity scatter plot. This suggests that GBLA-19 enters cells through lipid raft-mediated endocytosis. Besides endocytosis, endosomal escape is another challenging barrier during cytosolic protein delivery. If the complexes cannot escape from the endolysosomes after endocytosis, then the bound proteins will be degraded by proteases in the acidic vesicles. We therefore investigated the endosome escape capability of GBLA-19 and control polymers using LysoTracker Red to stain acidic organelles in the treated cells. A green pseudo-color was assigned to eYFP signals to better observe the colocalization. Cells treated with GBLA-19/eYFP complexes exhibited partial colocalization between eYFP and LysoTracker Red 1 hour after incubation (fig. S16). As incubation time prolonged, brighter eYFP signals appeared throughout the cells, which is in accordance with the time-dependent endocytosis results. Subsequently, the colocalization of GBLA-1, GBLA-3, GBLA-17, and GBLA-19 complexes with LysoTracker Red at 4 hours was measured by the same method. As shown in Fig. 3C, obvious yellow colocalization spots can be observed in cells treated with GBLA-1, GBLA-3, and GBLA-17 complexes. On the basis of the scatter plot of colocalization and a Pearson's correlation coefficient above 0.6, suggesting the entrapment of these nanoparticles in the acidic organelles after endocytosis. On the contrary, cells treated with GBLA-19/eYFP showed a Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.0699, indicating successful endosomal escape after 4-hour incubation. To quantitatively measure the endosomal escape capability of the polymers, a Gal8-YFP recruitment assay was performed. Galectin 8 (Gal8), a beta-galactoside carbohydrate-binding protein, was used to detect disrupted endosomes via binding to glycans located on the inner membrane of endosomes. The level of endosomal escape can be qualitatively measured by counting the number of yellow spots, indicating the extent of Gal8 recruitment within disrupted endosomes (Fig. 3D). As shown in Fig. 3 (E and F), HeLa cells stably expressing Gal8-YFP treated by GBLA-19/bovine serum albumin (BSA) complexes showed the highest Gal8 recruitment, while negligible yellow spots were observed for the other complex treated cells. Together, NBC- and LA-biofunctionalized polymer GBLA-19 exhibited remarkable efficacies in protein binding, endocytosis, responsive protein release, and endosomal escape and therefore indicated the superior performance in the synthesized polymer library.

Cytosolic delivery of bioactive proteins

We further tested the capability of GBLA series polymers in the cytosolic delivery of other bioactive proteins, including antibodies, enzymes, and Cas9 RNP complexes. IgG labeled with fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) was tested as a model antibody. After incubating HeLa cells with polymer/IgG-FITC complexes for 4 hours, it was observed that GBLA-15, GBLA-18, GBLA-21, and GBLA-22 significantly increased the cytosolic delivery of IgG-FITC compared to control or other complex formulations (Fig. 4B). These four polymers were further used for the delivery of nuclear pore complex (NPC) monoclonal antibody (anti-NPC). NPC is a channel composed of multiple proteins that control the transport of important biomolecules such as RNA and proteins between the cell nucleus and cytoplasm. Anti-NPC can specifically recognize and bind to NPC, leading to its inactivation and blocking of molecular transport. The distribution of internalized antibodies can be observed by immuno-fluorescence staining with fluorescently labeled secondary antibodies (Fig. 4A). To confirm the successful delivery of Anti-NPC into living cells, HeLa cells were incubated for 24 hours with polymer/anti-NPC complexes, then fixed, permeabilized, and incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled secondary antibody for 1 hour to visualize the internalized antibody by laser scanning confocal microscopy (LSCM). As shown in Fig. 4C, the cells treated with GBLA-18, GBLA-21, and GBLA-22 complexes clearly showed fluorescence specifically localized around the nucleus, demonstrating that anti-NPC was delivered into the cells and released from the complexes to exert their biofunction. We subsequently investigated the potential of GBLA polymers in the delivery of enzymes. beta-Gal is an enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of non-color substrate 5-bromo-4-chloro-3-indolyl-beta-d-galactoside (X-Gal) into a blue-colored product (Fig. 4D). Therefore, the beta-Gal delivery efficiency by GBLA polymers can be evaluated using the X-Gal in situ staining assay. After screening, a similar trend to cytosolic eYFP delivery was observed (Fig. 4E). Quantitatively, GBLA-18 exhibited the highest beta-Gal delivery efficacy into HeLa cells, which is about 70-fold higher than that of free beta-Gal (Fig. 4F). Because of the distinct molecular weight, hydrophilicity and isoelectric point (pI), the optimal NBC and LA grafting ratios for each cargo protein are slightly shifted. However, a similar trend was obtained for all the investigated proteins, that is, higher NBC and LA grafting ratios are usually required for more efficient cytosolic protein delivery. These results demonstrated that the GBLA polymer library can be used to screen optimal carriers for specific cargo protein delivery with reserved bioactivity.

For Cas9 RNP delivery, 293 T cells expressing enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) were treated with GBLA/Cas9 RNP complexes targeting EGFP. The commercial reagent Lipofectamine CRISPRMAX (CMAX) was tested as a positive control (Fig. 5A). As shown in Fig. 5B and fig. S17, flow cytometry analysis showed that 293 T-EGFP cells treated with GBLA-18, GBLA-19, GBLA-21, and GBLA-22 complexes exhibited an obvious increase in the percent of negative cells, suggesting efficient EGFP gene editing in the cells. In contrast, the fluorescence intensity and negative cell proportion of cells treated with RNP alone are scarcely changed. In addition to flow cytometry analysis, the T7 endonuclease I (T7E1) digestion assay was conducted to further confirm the disruption of the genome at the EGFP site in the treated cells mediated by the four GBLA complexes. Figure 5C shows that the treatment of 293 T-EGFP cells with GBLA-22/RNP resulted in a 34.5% indel efficiency, which is considerably higher than the indel efficiency achieved by CMAX. We investigated the genome editing efficiency of GBLA/RNP complexes at different genomic loci. Among the polymers, the highest gene disruptions at the AAVS1 locus (22.5%) and HBB locus (23.8%) in 293 T cells were observed for the GBLA-22/RNP complex, which is also superior to the commercial reagent CMAX (Fig. 5, D and E). A similar phenomenon was observed in the mutant KRAS locus on SW-480 cells. As shown in Fig. 5F, GBLA-22/RNP delivery achieved an obvious indel efficiency at the mutant KRAS locus (39.8%). Collectively, the results demonstrated that the dual-responsive polymers GBLAs especially GBLA-22 can efficiently deliver Cas9 RNP into target cells to induce gene editing.
Intracellular Cas9 RNP delivery by GBLA.

(A) Schematic of intracellular Cas9 RNP delivery. (B) Screening of efficient GBLA for Cas9 RNP delivery on 293 T-EGFP cells analyzed by flow cytometry. (C) Indel efficiency of EGFP locus determined by T7E1 assay. Indel efficiency of (D) AAVS1 and (E) HBB genomic locus in 293 T cells by T7E1 assay. (F) Indel efficiency of mutant KRAS genomic locus in SW-480 cells analyzed by the T7E1 assay. The number under the figure means the indel efficiency (%) of every sample.
Treatment of psoriasis by GBLA-22/Cas9 RNP nanocomplexes

Previous studies revealed that NLRP3 inflammasome is considered to play a pivotal role in the development and progression of psoriasis, and genome editing of NLRP3 inflammasome could ameliorate the inflammatory symptoms of imiquimod induced-psoriasis. We further evaluated the delivery of GBLA-22/Cas9 RNP targeting NLPR3 in the treatment of imiquimod-induced psoriasis. To investigate whether the treatment of the GBLA-22/RNP complex could ameliorate the inflammatory symptoms (Fig. 6A), the psoriasis area and severity index (PASI) score was evaluated once every 2 days. As shown in Fig. 6 (A and C to F), subcutaneous injection of GBLA-22/RNP complex targeting NLPR3 greatly alleviated the severity of psoriasis symptoms, including erythema, scaling, and induration, and the therapeutic efficacy is comparable to clinically used calcipotriol ointment. GBLA-22/RNP complex treatment did not induce obvious body weight changes during the therapeutic time, indicating limited adverse effects of the GBLA-22/RNP complex (Fig. 6B). Furthermore, as shown in Fig. 6 (G and H), significantly reduced skinfold thickness and skin biopsy weight were observed after treatment with GBLA/RNP complex and calcipotriol ointment. Furthermore, the transepidermal water loss (TEWL) and skin hydration were determined to evaluate skin barrier functions. As shown in Fig. 6 (I and J), moderate decreased levels of TEWL and enhanced levels of skin hydration were observed after the GBLA/RNP complex treatment, indicating that part of the barrier function is repaired. The weight and size of the spleen were increased in the psoriatic mice induced by imiquimod cream due to the release of large amounts of inflammatory cytokines (Fig. 6, K and L). In contrast, subcutaneous injection of GBLA/RNP complex targeting NLRP3 decreased the size and weight of the spleen, which are similar to normal mice. Next, the indel efficiency of NLRP3 in vivo was determined by T7E1 assay. A substantial gene disruption at the NLRP3 locus (33.7%) in the psoriatic skin tissues was observed after GBLA-22/RNP complex treatment (Fig. 6M). Sanger sequencing results confirmed deletions, insertions, and substitutions at the NLRP3 locus. Furthermore, the deep sequencing result was consistent with the results of the T7E1 assay and Sanger sequencing (Fig. 6, N and O). Histological analysis of skin tissues showed noticeably decreased hyperplasia and inflammation infiltration in the GBLA-22/RNP complex group, as compared with the psoriatic mice without treatment (Fig. 7A). In addition, the thickness of stratum corneum, epidermis, and dermis layers were markedly decreased in the GBLA-22/RNP complex group (Fig. 7, B to D). We also measured the major psoriasis-related cytokines expressions including interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta), IL-18, IL-17, IL-12/23p40, and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) in the psoriatic mice after treatment. As shown in Fig. 7 (E to I), the most inhibitory effect on IL-1beta, IL-18, and TNF-alpha release was observed in the GBLA-22/RNP group among all the groups. In addition, the expression of IL-17 and IL-12/23p40 in skin homogenates was significantly reduced after GBLA-22/RNP treatment, which is similar to the calcipotriol ointment group. To investigate how nanoparticles cleared in vivo and their biological distribution, GBLA-22 was labeled with Cy5, which can be tracked using an in vivo imaging system. As shown in fig. S18, retention of Cy5 fluorescence in skin tissue can be still observed on the fifth day after subcutaneous injection of GBLA-22-Cy5/RNP complexes. At different time intervals, mice were sacrificed and major organs were collected and also imaged (fig. S18B). The result showed that positive signals were recorded from the skin and liver at days 1 to 5, indicating that the skin and liver are the main metabolic organs of nanoparticles. On the other hand, the recognition, phagocytosis, and transport of mononuclear phagocytic systems are generally considered to be the main way for nanoparticles to be cleared in vivo. Collectively, these results demonstrated the promising efficacy of the GBLA/RNP nanocomplex targeting NLRP3 in the treatment of psoriasis.

The scores were rated on a 0-to-4 scale as follows: 0, none; 1, slight; 2, moderate; 3, obvious; 4, very obvious. (G) Thickness of back skinfold. DISCUSSION

In this study, a library of dual-functionalized polymers was developed for efficient cytosolic protein delivery. Polymers with higher densities of both boronate and LA ligands generally show better performances in the cytosolic delivery of bioactive proteins including fluorescent proteins, antibodies, enzymes, and Cas9 RNP. Both ligands play essential roles in the protein binding, endosomal escape, and intracellular release processes during cytosolic delivery. The bound proteins can be released from the nanocomplex triggered by both GSH and H2O2 after endocytosis. The optimal boronate and LA grafting ratios depend on the property of cargo proteins, and thus, we can screen efficient carriers for specific proteins in the library. Detailly, GBLA-19 has higher delivery efficiency for eYFP (28.4 kDa, pI 5.8) with relatively low molecular weight and low pI. GBLA-18 exhibits the best delivery efficiency for beta-Gal (430 kDa, pI 5.0) and IgG (150 kDa, pI 6.8) with many relatively higher molecular weights. For positively charged proteins such as Cas9 (160 kDa, pI 9.1), GBLA-22 shows the highest delivery efficiency and it successfully ameliorates the symptoms in imiquimod induced-psoriasis by genome editing of NLRP3 in vivo. The materials provide a promising option for the cytosolic delivery of proteins and protein complexes for the treatment of various diseases. Although the treatment of model mice with psoriasis by the proposed nanoformulation has been proven to be effective, dendrimer-based nanocarriers are still in the research stage and cannot yet be used for clinical application due to their unclarified systemic toxicity and degradability. Furthermore, the lack of active targeting capabilities can lead to poor biodistribution, which may trigger undesirable gene editing in other organs. These nanomaterials need to be obtained through multistep reactions, making it difficult to accurately synthesize monodispersed polymers. On the other hand, the effect of cross-linking degree on protein delivery efficiency and cargo release efficiency should be investigated. These issues remain to be further explored to meet the needs of clinical translation in the future.

passages.text: MATERIALS AND METHODS
Materials

BSA and IgG were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, USA). Anti-NPC (catalog no. ab24609) and Alexa Fluor 488-labeled Goat Anti-Mouse IgG H&L (catalog no. ab150117) were brought from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). Ethylenediamine-cored generation 5 polyamidoamine dendrimer was bought from Dendritech (Midland, USA). 4-(Hydroxymethyl) phenylboronic acid pinacol ester, 4-nitrophenyl carbonochloridate, dicyclohexylcarbodiimide (DCC), and triethylamine (TEA) were brought from Adamas Reagent (Shanghai, China). Magnesium sulfate (MgSO4) and sodium carbonate (Na2CO3) were from Greagent Reagent (Shanghai, China). Hydrochloric acid (HCl) was from Guangzhou Chemical Reagent Factory (Guangzhou, China). LA was from Mackin Biochemical (Shanghai, China). H2O2 was purchased from Aladdin Biochemical Technology (Shanghai, China). beta-Gal was from J&K Scientific (Shanghai, China). 2-(2-Methoxy-4-nitrophenyl)-3-(4-nitrophenyl)-5-(2,4-disulfophenyl)-2H-tetrazolium sodium salt (WST-8), Hoechst 33342, Lysotracker red, beta-Gal staining kit, and blocking solution were from Beyotime Biotechnology (Shanghai, China). Trypan blue was from Sangon Biotech (Shanghai, China). Dulbecco's modified Eagle's medium (DMEM), RPMI 1640, penicillin-streptomycin, and trypsin-EDTA were obtained from Gibco Life Technologies. Fetal bovine serum (FBS) was from PAN-Seratech (Aidenbach, Germany). eYFP and CRISPR-Cas9 protein with a glutamate peptide tag (E20) were expressed and purified according to a standard protein expression protocol. Wild-type CRISPR-Cas9 protein was obtained from GenScript (Nanjing, China). CMAX was bought from Thermo Fisher Scientific (Massachusetts, USA). Imiquimod cream was from 3M Pharmaceuticals (Aldara; Leicestershire, UK). T7E1 enzyme and HiScribe T7 Quick High Yield RNA Synthesis Kit were from New England Biolabs (Massachusetts, USA). Calcipotriol ointment was purchased from LEO Laboratories Limited (Ireland). Single-guide RNAs (sgRNAs) including sgEGFP, sgAAVS1, sgHBB, sgKRAS, and sgNLRP3 were designed by an online tool (http://chopchop.cbu.uib.no/). Primers for in vitro transcription of sgRNAs are listed in table S2. Primers for the T7E1 assay are listed in table S3.
Synthesis and characterization of NBC

NBC was synthesized as a previously reported method (as described in fig. S1). Generally, dissolving 4-(hydroxymethyl) phenylboronic acid pinacol ester (1.17 g, 5.0 mmol) in 15 ml of anhydrous tetrahydrofuran (THF), 4-nitrophenyl chloroformate (1.12 g, 5.6 mmol), and TEA (1.40 ml, 10.0 mmol) dissolved in THF were subsequently dropped into above solution to stir for 5 hours at room temperature. After the reaction, the mixture solution was diluted with EA and sequentially washed with 1.0 M HCl, saturated Na2CO3 solution, and brine. Then, the crude product was obtained by filtration, drying, and concentration. Flash chromatography of the residue on silica gel was conducted using PE/EA (10/1, v/v) as eluent to produce white powders, NBC. The 1H NMR spectrum of NBC was obtained using a JNM-ECZ500R NMR spectrometer (Japan) with tetramethylsilane as the internal standard.
Synthesis of G5 dendrimer and NBC conjugates (GB)

GB was prepared by reacting dendrimer with NBC at various molar ratios (fig. S2). Briefly, the dendrimer and NBC were dissolved in anhydrous dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO) and N,N'-dimethylformamide (DMF), respectively, and mixed together with the addition of three equivalents of TEA. After overnight stirring, the resulting solution was dialyzed sequentially against DMF, and ultrapure water, respectively, to remove the unreacted NBC and the hydrolysate pinacol. The resulting polymer, GB, was obtained by lyophilization and further characterized by 1H NMR to calculate the NBC grafting ratios.
Synthesis of LAA

LAA was synthesized according to the following method (fig. S3A). Generally, LA (1.03 g, 5.0 mmol) and DCC (0.65 g, 3.0 mmol) were dissolved in 25 ml of anhydrous dichloromethane and stirred at room temperature for 24 hours. After the reaction, the by-product urea was removed by filtration to give a yellow stock solution of LAA, which is stored at 4 C until further use.
Synthesis of G5 dendrimer and LA conjugates (GLA)

GLA was synthesized by reacting G5 dendrimer with LAA at various feeding molar ratios (fig. S3). Briefly, the dendrimer was dissolved in anhydrous DMSO. Then, LAA stock solutions were added at different molar ratios of LAA to primary amines on dendrimer (10, 20, and 30%, respectively). Three equivalents of TEA were added to the above mixture and stirred at room temperature overnight. The resulting solutions were dialyzed sequentially against DMSO and ultrapure water for 3 days after the reaction, respectively. The resulting polymers were lyophilized to obtain GLA and further characterized by 1H NMR to calculate the LA grafting ratios (fig. S4). Similarly, NBC and LA dual-functionalized dendrimers were synthesized by reacting GB with LAA at various molar ratios as described above (figs. S4 to S9).
Expression and purification of eYFP and E20-tagged Cas9

eYFP and recombinant protein E20-tagged Cas9 were expressed in Escherichia coli. For eYFP, E. coli BL21 cells (CWBIO) transfected with plasmid pET-eYFP were cultured in Luria-Bertani broth medium with kanamycin (100 mug/ml) and induced by adding 1 mM isopropyl beta-d-1-thiogalactopyranoside (IPTG). Nickel-nitrilotriacetic acid (Ni-NTA) buffer [50 mM tris-HCl and 500 mM NaCl (pH 8.0)] was added to collected bacterial cells before mechanical lysis and centrifugation. The lysate was filtered through a 0.22-mum filter. Last, the protein was purified using a Ni-NTA affinity column. For the recombinant protein E20-tagged Cas9, the protocol was similar to that used for eYFP. The expression was performed in 2xYT media with ampicillin (100 mug/ml) and an induction condition of 1 mM IPTG. After IPTG induction for 16 hours, the Ni-NTA buffer containing HALT Protease Inhibitor was added to collected bacterial cells before mechanical lysis and centrifugation. The supernatant was collected and dialyzed to decrease NaCl concentration. Proteins were purified using a HiTrap SP-HP column (GE Healthcare, USA) and concentrated using a concentrator column (Millipore, USA).
Synthesis of fluorescence-labeled IgG

Briefly, 5 mg of IgG was dissolved in PBS with the addition of FITC dissolved in DMSO (39 mul at a concentration of 1 mg/ml). The reaction solution was stirred at 4 C for 24 hours in the dark. After the reaction, the solution was dialyzed against PBS for 2 days to remove DMSO and unreacted FITC, and then lyophilized to acquire FITC-labeled IgG as yellow powders. The labeled antibody was resuspended in sterile water and stored at -20 C until further use.
Preparation and characterization of nanocomplexes

Briefly, different cargo proteins were complexed with GBLA polymers at different weight ratios, and then incubated in 50 mul of sterile water for 30 min. The assembled nanoparticles were diluted for further characterization using DLS (Zetasizer Nano ZS 90, Malvern, UK) and TEM (JEM-1400 Flash, JEOL, Japan) or an experiment of delivery protein binding and release assay. Generally, 10 mug of polymers was mixed with 6 mug of eYFP in test tubes, incubated with 50 mul of deionized water for 30 min, and further diluted to 250 mul of sterile water or PBS. The diluted samples were centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 20 min to separate complexes and unbound protein. Subsequently, the supernatant was pipetted and diluted to 1 ml in deionized water or PBS buffer. The fluorescence intensity of the diluted solution was determined by a fluorescence spectrophotometer (F-320, China). Free eYFP solution at the same concentration was conducted as a control. The protein loading efficiency (%) of each polymer was calculated according to the standard curve of eYFP in different media (fig. S12).

For the protein release assay, the GBLA/eYFP complexes were prepared as described above, and then diluted with 5 mM H2O2 or 5 mM GSH in PBS buffer to a total volume of 1 ml. The tubes were then centrifuged at 13,000 rpm for 20 min to separate the complexes and released proteins. Subsequently, the released proteins (%) were calculated by measuring the fluorescence intensity of the supernatant according to the standard curve.
Electrophoresis

The cross-linking of GBLA polymers was analyzed using SDS-PAGE. The polymers were first mixed with a nonreducing loading buffer, then loaded onto a concentration gel to run for 20 min at 80 V, and further electrophoresed by a separation gel at 120 V for 60 min. Once the electrophoresis was completed, the gel was stained with Coomassie brilliant blue and subsequently decolorized using deionized water containing 10% (v/v) acetic acid and 30% (v/v) methanol. Last, the gel was photographed using a transilluminator (BLT GelView 5000pro, China).
Cytosolic protein delivery

HeLa cells, 293 T cells, and SW-480 cells were bought from the American Type Culture Collection. HeLa cells were seeded in 48-well plates and 35-mm glass bottom dishes (NEST, China) overnight until the cell confluence reached 80 to 90%. The complexes were prepared by mixing polymers (40 mug/ml) and eYFP (24 mug/ml) together as described above, incubated in 50 mul of medium for 30 min, and added with another 200 mul of serum-free medium to dilute the complex before addition into the wells. After treatment for 4 hours, the culture media were replaced with 0.02% (w/v) trypan blue dissolved in PBS buffer to quench the fluorescence from proteins outside cells. The treated cells were directly imaged using a fluorescence microscope (Leica DM IL, Germany) and LSCM (Zeiss LSM880, Germany) equipped with an argon laser. For quantitative analysis, the treated cells were collected and resuspended in PBS before analysis by flow cytometry (BD FACSVerse, USA). Every sample was conducted in three parallel measurements. Naked proteins without any polymer were tested as a negative control. Cytosolic IgG-FITC into HeLa cells was conducted by the same procedures.

For beta-Gal delivery, HeLa cells were seeded in 48-well plates overnight before treatment with GBLA/beta-Gal complex (10 mug of GBLA and 6 mug of beta-Gal). Then, the intracellular beta-Gal enzyme activity was determined using a commercial kit. Each sample was conducted in three parallel measurements.

For cytosolic anti-NPC delivery, HeLa cells were seeded in a glass bottom dish overnight until the cell confluence reached 60 to 70%. The complexes were prepared by mixing 40 mug of polymers and 2.5 mug of anti-NPC, incubated for 30 min in 250 mul of medium. Another 1 ml of medium was further supplemented to dilute the complex before addition to the dish. After treatment for 24 hours, the cultured cells were subsequently washed with PBS three times, fixed with 4% (v/v) polyformaldehyde for 10 min at room temperature, and washed with PBS three times. The cells were permeabilized with 0.25% (v/v) Triton X-100 and 2% (w/v) BSA in PBS buffer for 5 min at room temperature. After washing with PBS, the cells were treated with blocking solution for 1 hour at room temperature to decrease nonspecific immunostaining and incubated with Alexa Fluor 488-labeled goat anti-mouse IgG at 1/1000 dilution for 1 hour and Hoechst 33342 for 10 min to visualize intracellularly anti-NPC and the nucleus, respectively. The cells were then imaged by LSCM.
Cell viability assay

The cytotoxicity of polymers on HeLa cells was assessed by a standard CCK-8 assay. Generally, HeLa cells were seeded on 96-well plates overnight, and then treated with polymers at a concentration range of 0 to 80 mug/ml. Then, media were replaced with fresh DMEM containing 10% FBS after incubation for 4 hours, and the cells were further incubated for another 20 hours. Afterward, 10 mul of CCK-8 solution was added into each well to incubate for 1 hour at 37 C. The absorbance of samples was measured at 450 nm with a reference wavelength of 650 nm by a microplate reader.

passages.text: Endocytosis and intracellular localization

Generally, HeLa cells were pretreated with Cyto D (10 muM), Gen (700 muM), MbetaCD (10 mM), CPZ (20 muM), and DTNB (2.4 mM) for 1 hour in DMEM medium at 37 C, and then incubated with GBLA/eYFP complexes for 4 hours as described above. The cells treated without any inhibitor were tested as a control. The treated cells were analyzed by flow cytometry, and the intracellular localization of eYFP was observed by LSCM. The nuclei and acidic organelles were stained with Hoechst 33342 and LysoTracker Red, respectively.
Gal8-YFP recruitment assay

Gal8-YFP recruitment assay was performed according to a previous reference. Briefly, HeLa cells with stably expressing Gal8-YFP fusion protein (HeLa-Gal8-YFP) were seeded in 35-mm glass bottom dishes overnight. The cells were then treated with GBLA/BSA complexes [GBLA (40 mug/ml) and BSA (24 mug/ml)] for 4 hours, imaged by LSCM, and the counts of yellow dots in the cells were quantified by ImageJ.
Gene editing assay

293 T cells stably expressing EGFP (293 T-EGFP) were seeded in 24-well plates 1 day before the gene editing experiment. Cas9/sgRNA RNP was assembled by incubating 1.5 mug of E20-Cas9 with 0.36 mug of sgRNA (equivalent to a 1:1.2 molar ratio) in 25 mul of Opti-MEM I medium containing 10x Cas9 Plus Reagent for 10 min at 37 C. Then, 10 mug of GBLA polymer was mixed with the prepared RNP gently by pipetting and incubated at 37 C for another 30 min, followed by dilution with 250 mul of DMEM. CMAX was conducted as a positive control according to the recommended protocol. When the cells reached 40% confluence, GBLA/Cas9 RNP complexes prepared by the above methods were added into the wells. Two hundred fifty microliters of complete media was added at 6 and 24 hours, respectively. The expression of EGFP in the cells was analyzed by flow cytometry after 48-hour incubation. Another group of experiments was also performed as described above for the T7E1 assay in vitro. Generally, the genomic DNA of treated cells was extracted 2 days after delivery by a TIANamp Genomic DNA Kit (TIANGEN) according to the standard protocols. The genomic DNA was transcribed with two pairs of specific polymerase chain reaction (PCR) primers (table S2) and EmeraldAmp MAX PCR Master Mix (Takara Bio, Japan) to obtain substrates for T7E1 assay. The digestion results of the T7E1 assay were evaluated with 2% (w/v) agarose gel electrophoresis. The disrupted genes were imaged by a transilluminator and quantitatively analyzed by ImageJ.

The gene editing experiments for AAVS1 and HBB in 293 T cells and KRAS in SW-480 cells were conducted in DMEM or Leibovitz's L-15 medium, respectively. The Cas9 RNP delivery process and T7E1 assay were the same as described above.
Imiquimod-induced psoriatic mouse model and treatment

Female BALB/c mice (6 to 8 weeks old) were kept under specific pathogen-free conditions. All animal experiments were carried out in accordance with the guidelines of the Laboratory Animal Welfare and Ethics Committee of Zhejiang University. Detailly, 30 mice were randomly divided into five groups, including normal control group (G1), imiquimod modeling group (G2), Cas9 RNP alone treatment group (G3), GBLA/Cas9 RNP complex treatment group (G4), and calcipotriol ointment treatment group (G5). Psoriatic model mice were established by topical stimulation of the shaved skin in a 2 cm x 2 cm area with 100 mg of 5% imiquimod cream every day for seven consecutive days. Four hours after imiquimod cream administration, GBLA/RNP nanocomplexes including 20 mug of Cas9 and 40 mug of GBLA-22 were subcutaneously injected into the psoriatic skin on the back through two-point injection at the upper and lower parts of the area every 3 days for treatment. Calcipotriol ointment was topically applied once every day. Clinical PASI score was evaluated on the basis of three pathological symptom factors, including erythema, scaling, and induration. The scores were rated on a 0-to-4 scale as follows: 0, none; 1, slight; 2, moderate; 3, obvious; 4, very obvious. The values of TEWL and skin hydration were determined by Tewameter TM 210 and Corneometer CM 820, respectively. At the end of the experiment, the skin tissues and spleen were collected for hematoxylin and eosin staining and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay.
T7E1 assay, Sanger sequencing, and deep sequencing

After the treatment, the skin tissues were collected and the genome DNA was extracted using the FastPure Cell/Tissue DNA Isolation Mini Kit (Vazyme Biotech) following the standard protocol. The T7E1 assay, Sanger sequencing, and deep sequencing of the skin tissues were processed and analyzed according to the reference.
Statistical analysis

The experiments were repeated three times and data were represented as means +- SD if not specially indicated. Student's t test was used for statistical analysis of significant differences. A value of P < 0.05 was considered significant. n.s., P > 0.05; *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, and ****P < 0.0001.
